case_title: Kilakkatha Parambath Sasi & Ors. v. State of Kerala
accused_victim_relationship: Political rival (alleged): accused described as members of one political party, victim and his brother as workers of a rival party. No other prior connection stated.
statutory_provisions: IPC ss.147, 148, 307, 324, 302 r/w s.149 (charged); four appellants convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34
weapon: Sword, axe and knife; the prosecution also suggested accused nos.5 to 7 were armed with a crow bar and sticks
evidence_type: Eyewitness (injured brother and passengers/independent witnesses); medical (post-mortem and injury examination); FIR and promptness of recording; seizure of bus trip-sheet (documentary)
aggravating_circumstances: Deceased suffered 58 injuries, most incised and cutting, some of huge dimensions; attack by a group allegedly motivated by political animosity
high_court_outcome: Acquittal reversed for four accused (Sasi, Dasan, Ashokan, Babu): convicted under IPC s.302 r/w s.34 and sentenced to life imprisonment; acquittal of the other three maintained
offence_finally_established: Murder under IPC s.302 r/w s.34
neutral_facts: Around mid-afternoon the victim and his brother boarded the same bus, having met by chance, with about ten to fifteen other passengers on board. Shortly after the bus reached a bus stand, the accused allegedly threatened to kill them and pushed both men off the bus onto the road. Other men ran from a nearby shop. Weapons were handed over, and the accused allegedly used a sword, an axe and a knife, while further men were said to have caused injuries with a crow bar and sticks. The brother received three incised wounds. The victim suffered 58 injuries, most of them incised and cutting wounds, some of large size, and died in hospital later that day. Police reached the scene about an hour after the incident and took the injured to hospital. The brother's statement was recorded at the hospital at about 5.30 p.m., and a formal report was registered at 7.15 p.m. and sent to the magistrate that night. The prosecution alleged that the assault arose from political rivalry between the groups involved. Evidence presented included the injured brother's account, statements from two passengers on the bus, an independent autorickshaw driver who said he witnessed the incident while getting his vehicle repaired, medical evidence from the post-mortem and from the examination of the brother, and the investigating officer's evidence that he had seized the bus trip-sheet. The bus crew were not examined as witnesses.
physical_harm: Victim (brother) died from 58 mostly incised and cutting wounds; injured witness PW-1 had three incised wounds
premeditation_planning: Not found by the Supreme Court. Prosecution alleged an unlawful assembly was formed and the attack occurred when the victims got off the bus; defence argued the accused were involved after deliberation.
motive: alleged: political animosity between the accused's party and the victim's party (Congress workers)
key_evidence_accepted: Injured eyewitness PW-1's account; PW-2 presence accepted though not named in FIR (named as present at hospital); PW-3 categoric eyewitness statement; PW-4 independent autorickshaw driver; promptly recorded FIR; medical evidence; seized trip-sheet
witness_credibility: PW-1 is an injured witness whose presence cannot be disputed and who was not an active political worker, so false implication appeared remote; PW-4 is truly independent with no reason to discard his evidence; PW-2's absence from the FIR does not mean he was not present; the Trial Court's doubts were held farfetched
trial_duration: offence: 24 March 1994; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 23.05.2003; Supreme Court: 4 February 2011
legal_representation: Accused/appellants: U.R. Lalit (senior counsel), E.M.S. Anam, Fazlin Anam. State of Kerala: Dinesh Dwivedi, G. Prakash, Beena Prakash, V. Senthil
investigation_status: FIR registered on the injured witness's statement; investigation completed; accused charged under IPC
procedural_irregularity: Bus crew not examined although the investigating officer seized the trip-sheet; the Supreme Court held this not fatal to the prosecution. The Trial Court's finding of FIR delay was held perverse.
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted all seven. High Court: acquittal reversed for four (convicted under s.302 r/w s.34, life imprisonment); acquittal of three upheld. Supreme Court: appeal dismissed.
prosecution_argument: High Court interference was justified because the trial judgment was perverse; there was no delay in lodging the FIR; PW-1, an injured witness, cannot be doubted, and not naming all seven at first was of no consequence since the three unnamed accused were acquitted
defence_argument: Unexplained FIR delay allowed the prosecution to fabricate a story against innocent persons; three accused were apparently not present; eyewitness accounts were discrepant and contradicted by medical evidence; PW-2 was not named in the FIR; bus crew not examined; the facts did not justify interference in an appeal against acquittal
legal_principle_applied: Appellate court should not interfere with acquittal save in exceptional cases, and only if the trial findings are not borne out by the evidence and are perverse; but the High Court may re-appraise evidence and must interfere if the trial findings were not possible on the evidence to avoid travesty of justice
precedent_relied_upon: Arulvelu and Anr. v. State represented by the Public Prosecutor and Anr., (2009) 10 SCC 206
